sources.title: Görg, Jacobs, Meuchelböck (2023), Who Is to Suffer? Quantifying the Impact of Sanctions on German Firms, IZA DP 16146 (Kiel Institute)
sources.what: German firm-level data on the 2014 sanctions. Total sales fell only for firms with more than 5% of sales in Russia (283 of about 8,000 exporters), by 4.8% at the 2015 peak, and the gap was no longer significant by 2017. Firms with less than 2% of sales in Russia showed no drop in total sales, which the authors read as 'able to divert their sales destined for Russia either to other destination countries or to the domestic market' (pp. 25-28, Figure 1)

sources.title: VATT Data Room report 3/2023 (Toikka, Laasonen, Toivanen): Russian invasion of Ukraine has had only minor economic effects on Finnish firms that used to trade with Russia
sources.what: Former Russia exporters: total exports fell relative to controls right after February 2022, but turnover was almost unaffected; no effect on employment or the wage bill

sources.title: Bank of Finland Bulletin 2024/3 (Simola): The collapse of trade with Russia has had a limited effect on Finnish manufacturing
sources.what: 'most the loss in Russian exports has been compensated for by penetration of new markets'; Russia was 5% of Finnish goods exports in 2021; Finnish exporters to Russia fell from over 2,000 (2019) to about 100 (end-2023)

sources.title: Gavoille (Latvijas Banka), How did Latvian firms exposed to Russia adapt to trade sanctions? (LSM, 10 June 2025), summarising the Latvijas Banka working paper 'Short drop or sudden stop?'
sources.what: Low-exposure exporters 'generally maintained (or even increased) turnover levels'; surviving firms with more than 25% of turnover from Russia cut employment by about 10%, and closures rose for that group

sources.title: de Lucio, Mínguez, Minondo, Requena, Reducing trade with Russia: Sanctions vs. firms' voluntary suspension of activities (Journal of International Economics, 2026), summary
sources.what: Spanish customs data: rerouting through neighbouring countries was only about 5% of exports lost in Russia. This covers rerouting to Russia, not sales to new buyers, so it does not measure redirection

proposals.note: No study gives the share of lost 2022 Russia sales that was redirected, either economy-wide or per country. I checked ECB, Bundesbank, Banca d'Italia and CEPR/VoxEU (the CEPR pages blocked access) and found none. The firm-level evidence points one way: losses were concentrated in the few firms that depended on Russia, and other exporters found other buyers or the home market. That supports a slightly lower default and Finland. Large diversified exporters stay at 0.35 because the German 2014 evidence shows real but small and temporary losses. The product (value kept × extra) for the default moves from about 0.27 to about 0.23 at a value kept of 0.67.

sources.title: Council ST-15232-2022-ADD-1 (MFA+ declaration: member states pay the interest, by GNI key, to end-2027)
sources.what: Who pays the MFA+ interest

proposals.note: Lender's cost = 1 - PV of Ukraine's interest and principal payments × (1 - expected loss), discounted at the lender's own funding rate: the EU's reported cost of funding; about 3% for other G7 lenders and 0.5% for Japan (judgement, not sourced). Scenarios: low = interest subsidy ends 2027 and expected loss 0; central = subsidy to 2034 and expected loss 10%; high = subsidy for the loan's life and expected loss 25%. The expected loss is judgement: Ukraine cut the face value of its private Eurobonds by 37% in 2024 but has kept paying official creditors. Weighted by face over all 140 loan items: 0.15/0.32/0.52. Without the 8.37bn Ukraine Support Loan defence window, which Kiel books as military and not under loans_face: 0.09/0.26/0.47. Without the whole Support Loan: 0.06/0.23/0.45. So the old 0.3 sits inside the range and close to the central value; the data mainly add the range and a per-class split. Japan's IBRD guarantees (9.6bn) cost Japan almost nothing unless Ukraine defaults on the IBRD, so a single scalar overstates Japan's cost (about 0.05 instead of 0.3).

sources.what: About CAD 9.5m remitted June 2022 to February 2026 in total; about CAD 1.2m expected per year

proposals.note: Arithmetic. EU: the Commission's estimates are EUR 65.6m (2022) and EUR 48.4m (2023) a year, against EU27 purchases from Ukraine in 2021 of EUR 25.07bn (site/data.json buy_ukr). That gives 0.26% and 0.19%. The central value of 0.3% adds a little because 2022-24 above-quota volumes (sugar, wheat, poultry) were far above 2021. The high value of 1% is a judgement: duties on the actual surge volumes would be much higher, but at those duties the volumes would not have come, so it is not revenue given up. UK: 1.4% of imports carried duty × an assumed 10-30% duty on those goods (not sourced) = 0.14-0.42%, so 0.2% central. Canada: CAD 9.5m (about EUR 6.6m at roughly 1.45 CAD/EUR) over EUR 0.62bn of purchases from Ukraine in June 2022 to February 2026 = 1.1%. The first year was about 3.3% (CAD 7.5m against about EUR 0.16bn) and the later years about 0.3%. At the old 4%, the EU's cost was about EUR 1.0bn a year. The Commission's own estimate is EUR 0.05-0.07bn. About 75% of EU customs duties go to the EU budget (25% is kept for collection costs), so the EU part could be split by EU budget share instead of by each member's imports. Not found: the Commission's ex-post figure for duties actually waived in 2022-2025, and a UK figure after 2022.
